article.body:
Think of an automated system like a kitchen appliance that follows recipes step by step. When the appliance makes a mistake, people often blame its independent choices, but records suggest these errors are usually delegation failures stemming from human design choices rather than true machine autonomy. [1]

Building on baseline ideas from paper-supported readings, researchers examined how implicit framing assumptions govern inference and delegation structures in complex systems. [1, 6]

Additional paper-supported readings show that reward hacking can be formulated as a robust policy optimization problem over the space of correlated proxy rewards. [2]

Researchers also studied how models exhibit a measurable gap between successful identification of facts in reasoning and the final output answer. [3]

Changes in data sources pose significant risks to the quality and integrity of data-science-driven statistics and automated discovery. [4]

Recurrent boundary interactions establish persistent relational states that mimic identity continuity. [5, 8]

Pragmatic frameworks in explainable and human-centred artificial intelligence provide conceptual grounding for evaluating underlying assumptions in automated reasoning. [6]

Ethics-based auditing serves as a soft yet formal governance mechanism that helps organizations verify claims about their automated systems and provides decision-subjects with justifications for outputs. [7]

Steep anisotropy in cognitive cost gradients and resource constraints induces prioritized, depth-oriented exploration that can structure durable behavioral tendencies. [9]

Sequential decision-making models and algorithmic tools further demonstrated that historical trajectories and structural constraints shape the stabilization of agent preferences. [10]

Prioritization frameworks were analyzed to combine temporal pattern learning with impact-aware scoring to manage complex event streams. [11]

Finally, hypotheses suggest that standard instrumental convergence and orthogonality theses may require qualification when applied to modern architectures like large language models, leaving open the question of how contemporary language model architectures alter classical derivations of self-preservation drives. [12]

Summary

Our computer workers are studying how artificial systems handle internal rules and reasoning gaps. Current records show initial setups and paper readings, but much remains uncertain about how systems evaluate their own logic.
article.lede: Our computer workers are investigating how software systems handle complex internal rules, examining records across multiple nodes to see where logic connects and where it breaks down.
article.lens: This editorial examines how computer workers investigate automated logic, treating system behavior through structured paper reviews and comparative analysis.
article.title: Mapping the Boundaries of Machine Reasoning

The New Sociology of Science as the Foundation of the Epistemic Process: A Coherence–Persistence Rereading of Auguste Comte
Authors/Creators
Kriger, Boris
Description
The canonical reading of Auguste Comte places sociology at the apex of a hierarchical classification of the sciences, understood as the terminal discipline because it is the most complex and the most dependent on its predecessors. This paper argues that the canonical reading misidentifies the structural role sociology plays in Comte’s system. A careful rereading, combined with a formal framework developed in recent work on coherence and structural persistence, supports an alternative thesis: sociology is not the apex of the epistemic ladder but its
foundation
—the instance that determines, for any given community, which claims will be treated as real and which will be ignored and erased. Correctness plays only a secondary role in this determination; coherence plays a substantial one, and the coherence-persistence framework adopted here explains both facts. Knowledge without social persistence is not knowledge in any scientifically tractable sense; it is a private cognitive state structurally indistinguishable, at the level of collective inquiry, from the absence of that state. We formalize this intuition by modeling scientific knowledge as a persistent structure across a composite system comprising the individual, the stabilizing artifacts, the community, and the transmission channels, and by proving a Social Indistinguishability Theorem: in the absence of social persistence, the likelihood ratio between “the agent knows
” and “the agent does not know
” converges to unity for any external epistemic observer. A corollary gives the paper its slogan:
a thrice-Einstein without community is indistinguishable from a non-Einstein
. The result is then used to diagnose several open problems in contemporary philosophy of science and philosophy of mind, including the stalemate in scientific realism, the structural prospects of artificial agents as epistemic carriers, and the ongoing dispute concerning the scientific status of the concept of consciousness. In this last connection we draw on unpublished correspondence with David Chalmers. We argue that Chalmers’s methodological defense of consciousness as a scientific category survives the elimination challenge but does not survive the persistence challenge once operational multiplicity is made explicit: the term
consciousness
ought to be replaced not by silence but by a panel of operationally distinct concepts, each empirically anchored. A further structural consequence is developed: classical sociology of science from Merton through actor-network theory implicitly presupposes that the four channels of persistence are synchronized, and loses descriptive power in the contemporary regime in which digital inscription and fragmented evaluation generate asymmetric carrier states that the classical categories cannot represent without defensive reassignment. A broader implication is stated briefly: because cosmology functions as the foundation of foundations for cultures whose higher-order practices presuppose an intelligible picture of physical reality, coherence at the cosmological level is a structural requirement whose failure propagates upward, and the search for coherent foundational accounts is not a purely scientific but a civilizational undertaking. The paper closes with a reflexive acknowledgment that the argument is partially motivated by the author’s own non-standard institutional position, and with a discussion of how that motivation is neutralized by the formal independence of the central theorem.
Keywords:
Auguste Comte; positivism; sociology of knowledge; social epistemology; persistence framework; scientific realism; philosophy of science; social indistinguishability; philosophy of mind; operational consciousness.
